q: This opera house on Bennelong Point is topped with sail-like white shells. It was designed by the Danish architect Jørn Utzon and opened in 1973. For 10 points, name this landmark of an Australian harbor city.
This Catalan architect designed the Casa Batlló and Park Güell. His unfinished church, the Sagrada Família, is full of curves and nature-inspired forms. For 10 points, name this Barcelona architect.

This building at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue was designed by James Hoban and has been the home of presidents since John Adams. It was burned by the British in 1814. For 10 points, name this building in Washington, DC.

This sixth-century church in Constantinople was commissioned by Justinian and features a giant dome supported on pendentives. It was later turned into a mosque, with minarets added. For 10 points, name this Byzantine building in Istanbul.

This German-American architect said "Less is more" and designed the Seagram Building in New York City. His steel-and-glass buildings include Crown Hall and the Barcelona Pavilion. For 10 points, name this Bauhaus director.

This curved structure spans an opening and is held together at the top by a wedge-shaped stone called the keystone. The Romans used it widely in bridges and aqueducts. For 10 points, name this structure also seen at the McDonald's logo.

This Greek column style is topped with a capital decorated with acanthus leaves. Its columns are tall and slender. For 10 points, name this style, the most ornate of the three, which is the last in the sequence Doric, Ionic, and this one.

This tilting bell tower stands in the Piazza dei Miracoli in Tuscany. It began leaning during construction because it was built on soft soil. Legend says Galileo dropped balls from it. For 10 points, name this campanile.
Salisbury Plain in England is the location of this prehistoric monument of huge standing stones in a circle. It aligns with the sun at the summer solstice. For 10 points, name this site.

This Inca citadel stands high in the Andes above the Urubamba River in Peru. It was abandoned and unknown to the outside world until Hiram Bingham brought attention to it in 1911. For 10 points, name this site.

This Swiss-French architect wrote that a house is "a machine for living in." He designed the Villa Savoye and the Unité d'Habitation. For 10 points, name this Swiss-French architect who wrote Toward an Architecture.

This Roman building in Rome has a huge concrete dome with an opening at the top called the oculus. It was rebuilt under Hadrian and later became a church. For 10 points, name this temple to all the gods.

In Gothic cathedrals, these exterior arched supports carry the thrust of the roof to heavy piers outside the walls. They allowed walls to be thinner and filled with windows. For 10 points, name these supports at Notre-Dame.

This red suspension bridge connects San Francisco with Marin County. It was opened in 1937 and is painted a color called International Orange. For 10 points, name this bridge across a strait of the same name.

This Art Deco skyscraper on Fifth Avenue in New York City opened in 1931. It has 102 floors and features a tall mast that was meant for airships. King Kong climbed it in a film. For 10 points, name this building.

This 1920s and 1930s style features geometric zigzags, sunbursts, and stylized ornament. The Chrysler Building is a famous example. For 10 points, name this style whose name comes from a Paris exposition of decorative arts.

This palace outside Paris was built by Louis XIV and has a Hall of Mirrors. Its gardens were designed by André Le Nôtre. The Treaty ending World War I with Germany was signed in it. For 10 points, name this palace.

This Canadian-American architect used curving sheets of titanium on the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao. He also designed the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles. For 10 points, name this deconstructivist architect.

This Chinese-American architect designed a glass pyramid for the courtyard of the Louvre. He also designed the East Building of the National Gallery of Art and the John Hancock Tower in Boston. For 10 points, name this architect.

This medieval fortress-palace sits on a hill above Granada, Spain, and was the last stronghold of the Moors. It has a Court of the Lions with a fountain on twelve statues. For 10 points, name this Nasrid complex.

This Gothic cathedral stands on an island in the Seine in Paris. Its towers, rose windows, and flying buttresses inspired Victor Hugo's novel about a hunchback named Quasimodo. A fire damaged its roof and spire in 2019. For 10 points, name this cathedral whose name means "Our Lady."

q: This London playhouse was built in 1599 on the south bank of the Thames by the company of Richard Burbage. Many plays by its resident playwright premiered there, and it burned down in 1613. A modern reconstruction stands nearby. For 10 points, name this round, open-air Elizabethan theater.

In this art form, dancers wear tutus and special shoes that let them stand on the tips of their toes. It developed in Renaissance Italy and was refined in France and Russia. Swan Lake and Giselle are classic examples. For 10 points, name this dance form with positions such as plié and arabesque.

This American photographer made black-and-white pictures of Yosemite Valley and the American West. He cofounded Group f/64 and developed the Zone System for controlling exposure. For 10 points, name this photographer of Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico.

This photographer worked for the Farm Security Administration during the Great Depression. Her photograph of a worried mother with her children in a pea-picker's camp is called Migrant Mother. For 10 points, name this woman.

This street in New York City runs through the theater district near Times Square. Musicals such as The Phantom of the Opera and The Lion King have long runs on its stages. For 10 points, name this theater center, whose name also refers to professional stage productions in New York.

These annual awards for live theater on Broadway are named for the actress Antoinette Perry. Winners receive a medal and are named in categories such as Best Musical and Best Play. For 10 points, name these awards.

This 2015 hip-hop musical by Lin-Manuel Miranda tells the story of a Treasury secretary who was born in the Caribbean. It features songs like "My Shot" and "The Room Where It Happens." For 10 points, name this musical about the first Secretary of the Treasury.

This choreographer founded a company in New York in 1926 and created a modern dance technique based on contraction and release of the torso. Her works include Appalachian Spring, with music by Aaron Copland. For 10 points, name this pioneer of modern dance.

This American choreographer founded a dance theater in 1958 whose best-known work is Revelations, set to spirituals. His company is based in New York City. For 10 points, name this African-American dance pioneer.

This Japanese art involves folding a single square sheet of paper into shapes without cutting it. A popular model is the crane, and legend says folding a thousand grants a wish. For 10 points, name this art.

In this craft, artists shape wet clay into forms like bowls and vases, often on a spinning wheel. The pieces are then dried and fired in a kiln, and many are covered with a glaze. For 10 points, name this craft.

This performance art relies only on gesture and facial expression, with no spoken words. Marcel Marceau made it famous with his character Bip, and a classic trick is pretending to be trapped in a box. For 10 points, name this silent art.

This Russian director and teacher cofounded the Moscow Art Theatre. His acting system asked actors to draw on emotional memory and objectives, and it inspired American method acting. For 10 points, name this author of An Actor Prepares.

This Japanese form of musical drama features performers in carved wooden masks and very slow, stylized movements. Plays are often about ghosts and are written by playwrights like Zeami. For 10 points, name this classical theater tradition.

This French artist and inventor developed a photographic process in the 1830s that fixed an image on a silvered copper plate. A picture made with it is named after him. For 10 points, name this man who worked with Joseph Nicéphore Niépce.

In ballet, this word names a quick spin on one foot, with the other leg raised to the side or held against the knee. It is French for "whirl," and dancers called fouettés repeat a related turn in Swan Lake. For 10 points, name this dance move.

This Italian theater form from the sixteenth century used stock characters like Harlequin and Pantalone, improvised dialogue, and masks. It means "comedy of the profession." For 10 points, name this tradition that influenced Moliere.

This art of beautiful handwriting uses pens with broad nibs or brushes and has traditions in Arabic, Chinese, and European scripts. Illuminated manuscripts by monks are a famous example. For 10 points, name this art.

In this art form, pieces of paper, cloth, photographs, and other flat materials are glued to a surface to make a composition. Picasso and Braque pioneered it in painting. For 10 points, name this technique whose name comes from the French for "glue."

In this style of dance, dancers wear shoes with metal plates on the heel and toe to make rhythmic sounds. Fred Astaire and Gene Kelly used it in movies, and Bill Robinson was a famous practitioner. For 10 points, name this dance.

This ballroom dance has three beats to a measure and a smooth, turning step. It became popular in Vienna in the nineteenth century, with music by Johann Strauss. For 10 points, name this dance in three-four time.
This passionate dance and song style from Andalusia in Spain features guitar, hand clapping, and fast footwork. Dancers sometimes use fans and castanets. For 10 points, name this Spanish art.

This German design school was founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919. It combined crafts and fine arts and taught that form should follow function. It later moved to Dessau. For 10 points, name this school that influenced modern architecture and design.

This art form makes images from tiny pieces of colored stone, glass, or tile called tesserae. Byzantine churches in Ravenna are famous for it, and Roman villas often had floors decorated with it. For 10 points, name this art.

In theater, this term names the area of the stage farthest from the audience. Stages were once built on a slope so that this area was higher. For 10 points, name this direction, the opposite of downstage.

This craft joins pieces of fabric, often with a batting layer between, using stitching in patterns. Women from Gee's Bend, Alabama, are famous for their patterns, and the Amish also made them. For 10 points, name this craft.

This urban dance style began in the Bronx in the 1970s alongside hip-hop music. It includes spins on the back or head and moves such as the windmill and the freeze. For 10 points, name this dance, also called b-boying.

This traditional Japanese theater features all-male casts, stylized makeup called kumadori, and a walkway through the audience called hanamichi. Actors known as onnagata play female roles. For 10 points, name this theater.
This French photographer, a cofounder of Magnum Photos, wrote about the "decisive moment" in photography. He photographed Paris street scenes with a small Leica camera. For 10 points, name this man.

The Tlingit, Haida, and other peoples of the Pacific Northwest carve these tall wooden poles from cedar. They display figures like ravens and bears that represent family histories. For 10 points, name this type of carved monument.

q: This river's delta includes the Atchafalaya Basin and is rapidly losing wetlands. Its tributaries include the Arkansas and the Ohio. It begins at Lake Itasca in Minnesota. For 10 points, name this longest river system in the United States by many measures, which flows through New Orleans to the Gulf of Mexico.

This canyon was carved over millions of years by a river and is more than a mile deep in places. Its South Rim is reached from the town of Tusayan. The Hualapai and Havasupai peoples live near it. For 10 points, name this Arizona landmark carved by the Colorado River.

This mountain range runs from New Mexico through Colorado and Wyoming to Montana, forming the Continental Divide. Pikes Peak and Longs Peak are in its Colorado section. Denver sits just east of it. For 10 points, name this North American mountain range.

This state was purchased from Russia in 1867 for about seven million dollars. Its capital is Juneau and its largest city is Anchorage. It is the largest state by area. For 10 points, name this northwesternmost state of the United States.
This state is made up of volcanic islands in the Pacific, including Maui, Kauai, and Oahu. Its capital is Honolulu. Pearl Harbor is on one of its islands. For 10 points, name this fiftieth state.

This lake is the largest of the Great Lakes by surface area. Its southern shore includes the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, and Duluth is a port on its western tip. The Edmund Fitzgerald sank in it in 1975. For 10 points, name this Great Lake.

This mountain range stretches from Georgia and Alabama north to Maine and Canada. The Blue Ridge and the Great Smoky Mountains are parts of it. A famous long hiking trail follows its crest. For 10 points, name this eastern mountain system.

This national park straddles the California and Nevada border and contains Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America. It is known for extreme summer heat. For 10 points, name this desert valley in the Mojave region.

This state is a peninsula with Miami on its southeast coast and Tallahassee as its capital. Walt Disney World and Cape Canaveral are located there. Its southern tip includes the Keys. For 10 points, name this southeastern "Sunshine State."
This state's capital is Austin, and its largest cities include Houston and Dallas. It borders Mexico along the Rio Grande. The Alamo is in San Antonio. For 10 points, name this "Lone Star State."
This lake in Utah is saltier than the ocean, so swimmers float easily. It is the remnant of the ancient Lake Bonneville. Antelope Island sits in it. For 10 points, name this lake near Salt Lake City.

This monument in the Black Hills of South Dakota features carved faces of four presidents. Gutzon Borglum directed its sculpting. The presidents shown include Washington and Lincoln. For 10 points, name this mountain monument.

This national park in Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho is home to the geyser Old Faithful. It was established in 1872 as the first national park in the United States. Bison and grizzly bears live there. For 10 points, name this park.

These waterfalls on the border of New York and Ontario include the American Falls and the Horseshoe Falls. The Maid of the Mist boat carries visitors close to them. The Niagara River flows over them. For 10 points, name these waterfalls.
This city on Lake Michigan is nicknamed the "Windy City." It is home to Wrigley Field and the Willis Tower. Its river was famously reversed in 1900. For 10 points, name this largest city in Illinois.

This river rises in Montana and flows southeast to join the Mississippi River near Saint Louis. Lewis and Clark traveled up it. It is nicknamed the "Big Muddy." For 10 points, name this longest river in the United States by length of its main stem.

This river carved the Grand Canyon and is dammed at Lake Mead and Lake Powell. It begins in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado. Its water is divided among several western states and Mexico. For 10 points, name this river that flows into the Gulf of California.
The highest mountain in North America, formerly named for a president, is found in this state. It lies in the Alaska Range. For 10 points, name this mountain, whose Native name means "the high one."

This flat grassland region of the central United States stretches from Texas to the Dakotas, east of the Rocky Mountains. Bison once roamed it in huge herds. The 1930s Dust Bowl struck it. For 10 points, name this region of prairie.

This Louisiana city sits near the mouth of the Mississippi River and is famed for jazz and Mardi Gras. Hurricane Katrina flooded it in 2005. Its French Quarter is a major attraction. For 10 points, name this city.

The capital of the United States is located in this district, which is not part of any state. It lies on the Potomac River between Maryland and Virginia. For 10 points, give the name of this district that includes the White House and the Capitol.

This is the only Great Lake located entirely within the United States. Chicago and Milwaukee lie on its shores. It is connected to Lake Huron by the Straits of Mackinac. For 10 points, name this lake.

This desert in southern California and Nevada contains Joshua trees and a national preserve. It lies between Los Angeles and Las Vegas. Barstow is in it. For 10 points, name this North American desert.

This state has the largest population in the United States. Sacramento is its capital, and it has the cities of Los Angeles and San Francisco. Its coast is on the Pacific Ocean. For 10 points, name this "Golden State."
This large wetland of sawgrass and mangroves is located in southern Florida. It is a national park home to alligators, manatees, and the Florida panther. For 10 points, name this "River of Grass."

This river forms the southern border of Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois. It joins the Mississippi River at Cairo, Illinois. Cincinnati and Pittsburgh are along it or its headwaters. For 10 points, name this river.

This inlet of the Pacific Ocean in Washington State includes Seattle and Tacoma on its shores. It was named for a lieutenant on George Vancouver's expedition. Ferries cross it to islands like Bainbridge. For 10 points, name this sound in the Pacific Northwest.

This dam on the Colorado River, on the Nevada-Arizona border, was completed in 1936. It created Lake Mead. It was built during the Great Depression. For 10 points, name this famous dam near Las Vegas.

This red suspension bridge connects San Francisco to Marin County. It opened in 1937 across a strait that leads to the Pacific Ocean. Fog often covers its towers. For 10 points, name this California bridge.

This peninsula in Massachusetts has a hooked shape and includes Provincetown at its tip. The Pilgrims first landed near its end in 1620. Its towns include Hyannis and Chatham. For 10 points, name this vacation destination on the Atlantic coast.

q: This river flows north through Uganda, Sudan, and Egypt and empties into the Mediterranean Sea through a large delta. The Blue Nile and White Nile join at Khartoum. The Aswan High Dam is on it. For 10 points, name this river of ancient Egypt.

This river in South America carries more water than any other river and flows through Brazil and Peru. Manaus lies on it. Its basin holds the largest tropical rainforest. For 10 points, name this river.

This is the largest hot desert in the world, covering much of northern Africa. Camels carry travelers across its dunes. It stretches from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea. For 10 points, name this desert.

Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first climbed this mountain in 1953. It lies on the border of Nepal and China. It is the highest mountain above sea level. For 10 points, name this peak in the Himalayas.
This country is both a continent and a nation. Its capital is Canberra, and its largest city is Sydney. Kangaroos and koalas live there. For 10 points, name this country in the Southern Hemisphere.
This island country in East Asia is made up of four main islands, including Honshu and Hokkaido. Its capital is Tokyo. Mount Fuji is its highest peak. For 10 points, name this country.

This country is the largest in South America and the only one where Portuguese is the main language. Its capital is Brasilia. Rio de Janeiro is its famous coastal city. For 10 points, name this country.
This country in northeastern Africa is home to the pyramids at Giza and the city of Cairo. The Suez Canal crosses it. Its ancient pharaohs ruled along the Nile. For 10 points, name this country.
This South Asian country has New Delhi as its capital and the Ganges as a sacred river. Its cities include Mumbai and Kolkata. The Taj Mahal is in Agra. For 10 points, name this country.

This mountain range separates the Indian subcontinent from the Tibetan Plateau. It includes Kangchenjunga. Nepal and Bhutan lie within it. For 10 points, name this range, home to the world's highest peaks.

This is the largest and deepest ocean, covering about a third of the Earth's surface. It contains the Mariana Trench and the Ring of Fire. It borders Asia and the Americas. For 10 points, name this ocean.

This continent around the South Pole is covered by a thick ice sheet and has no permanent residents. Penguins live on its coasts. Scientists staff research stations there. For 10 points, name this southernmost continent.

This country is the second largest in the world by area and has Ottawa as its capital. It has ten provinces and three territories. Toronto and Vancouver are its large cities. For 10 points, name this country north of the United States.
This country to the south of the United States has a capital built on the ruins of Tenochtitlan. Its language is Spanish. The Yucatan Peninsula is in it. For 10 points, name this country.

This country spans eleven time zones and is the largest in the world by area. Its cities include Saint Petersburg and Vladivostok. Moscow is its capital. The Trans-Siberian Railway crosses it. For 10 points, name this country.
This country's shape resembles a boot, and its capital is Rome. It contains the cities of Venice and Florence. Mount Vesuvius is near Naples. For 10 points, name this country in southern Europe.

This mountain range runs along the western edge of South America and is the longest continental mountain range. Machu Picchu was built in it. Aconcagua is its highest peak. For 10 points, name this range.
This coral system lies off the northeast coast of Queensland, Australia. It is made up of thousands of individual reefs. It can be seen from space. For 10 points, name this largest coral reef system.

This imaginary line circles the Earth at zero degrees latitude, dividing the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Ecuador is named for it. It passes through Kenya and Indonesia. For 10 points, name this line.

This is the largest island in the world that is not a continent. It is an autonomous territory of Denmark, and most of it is covered by ice. Nuuk is its capital. For 10 points, name this island northeast of Canada.

This island nation off the southeast coast of Africa is home to lemurs. Its capital is Antananarivo. It is the fourth largest island in the world. For 10 points, name this country in the Indian Ocean.

This waterway cuts across a narrow isthmus and links the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. It uses locks and opened in 1914. Ships pass through Gatun Lake. For 10 points, name this canal in Central America.

This sea is bordered by Spain, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Egypt, and Morocco. It connects to the Atlantic through the Strait of Gibraltar. Crete and Sicily are islands in it. For 10 points, name this sea.
This European mountain range includes Mont Blanc and the Matterhorn. It stretches across Switzerland, France, Italy, and Austria. Hannibal crossed it with elephants. For 10 points, name this range.

This capital of Egypt sits on the Nile near its delta. The Giza Pyramids are just outside it. Its Tahrir Square is famous, and its old district has the Khan el-Khalili bazaar. For 10 points, name this city.

This capital of Japan was once called Edo. The Imperial Palace is in it. The Shibuya crossing and the Sumida River are located there, and the Olympics were held there in 1964. For 10 points, name this city.

This city straddles Europe and Asia across the Bosphorus. It was once called Constantinople. The Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque stand there. A bridge across the strait connects its European and Asian sides. For 10 points, name this largest city in Turkey.
This landlocked country in the Alps is known for its neutrality and chocolate. Its cities include Zurich, Geneva, and Bern. Its flag is a white cross on red. For 10 points, name this country.

This mountain in Tanzania is the highest in Africa. It is a dormant volcano with snow near its top, and it has three volcanic cones named Kibo, Mawenzi, and Shira. Hikers climb it from towns like Moshi. For 10 points, name this peak.
This river is the longest in Asia and flows from the Tibetan Plateau through Chongqing and Wuhan to Shanghai. The Three Gorges Dam is on it. For 10 points, name this Chinese river.
This desert in Mongolia and northern China is cold and rocky. Genghis Khan's empire arose nearby, and dinosaur fossils have been found there. For 10 points, name this Asian desert.

q: Alexander Graham Bell is usually credited with patenting this device in 1876. His assistant Thomas Watson heard the first words spoken over it. It converts sound into electrical signals and back into sound. For 10 points, name this communication device that has a handset and a dial or keypad.

Thomas Edison developed a long-lasting version of this device in 1879 using a carbon filament. It glows when electric current heats a thin wire. Joseph Swan independently developed a similar one in England. For 10 points, name this lighting device that is screwed into a lamp.

Orville and Wilbur made the first sustained, powered flights of this type of vehicle at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903. Their first one was called the Flyer. It has wings and an engine or propeller. For 10 points, name this vehicle invented by the Wright brothers.

Johannes Gutenberg developed this machine in Germany around 1440, using movable metal type. His most famous product was a Bible with forty-two lines per page. It greatly increased the spread of books in Europe. For 10 points, name this invention.

Families gather on the fourth Thursday of November for this American holiday, which features turkey and pumpkin pie. It commemorates a harvest feast shared by the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag. Abraham Lincoln proclaimed it a national holiday during the Civil War. For 10 points, name this holiday.

On this holiday, which falls on October 31, children wear costumes and go trick-or-treating. Jack-o'-lanterns carved from pumpkins are common decorations. It grew from the Celtic festival of Samhain. For 10 points, name this autumn holiday.

Every four years, an extra day is added to February in this kind of year to keep the calendar aligned with the Earth's orbit. The year 2000 was one, but 1900 was not. People born on February 29 celebrate birthdays only in this kind of year. For 10 points, name this type of year with 366 days.

This statue on an island in New York Harbor was a gift from France in 1886. Frederic Bartholdi designed it, and Gustave Eiffel built its iron framework. It holds a torch and a tablet. For 10 points, name this symbol of liberty.

This sporting event was revived in 1896 in Athens by Pierre de Coubertin. Its symbol is five interlocking rings of different colors. It takes place every four years in summer and winter versions. For 10 points, name this international athletic competition that began in ancient Greece.

A Frenchman who lost his sight as a child developed this writing system in the 1820s. It uses patterns of raised dots arranged in cells. Readers feel the dots with their fingertips. For 10 points, name this reading system for people who are blind.

Samuel Morse helped develop this system for sending messages over telegraph wires. It uses combinations of short and long signals called dots and dashes. The distress signal SOS is famous in it. For 10 points, name this code.
This tower in Paris was built for the 1889 World's Fair. It is made of wrought iron and named for its engineer. It stands on the Champ de Mars. For 10 points, name this French landmark.

This long defensive structure in northern China was built and rebuilt by many dynasties, notably the Ming. Watchtowers dot its length. It stretches across mountains and deserts. For 10 points, name this wall.

This British passenger liner sank in the North Atlantic in April 1912 after striking an iceberg. It was said to be unsinkable on its maiden voyage from Southampton. More than 1,500 people died. For 10 points, name this ship.

This black stone slab, found in Egypt in 1799, was inscribed with the same decree in three scripts. Jean-Francois Champollion used it to decipher hieroglyphs. It is now kept in the British Museum. For 10 points, name this key to Egyptian writing.

Players of this board game for two move sixteen pieces each across sixty-four squares. Its pieces include the knight, bishop, and rook. The goal is to trap the opposing king. For 10 points, name this game, whose winning condition is called checkmate.

The Great Seal of the United States and many coins display this bird of prey. It has a white head and tail as an adult, and it appears on the Great Seal adopted in 1782. It eats fish. For 10 points, name this bird, the national emblem.

This bell in Philadelphia has a famous crack and bears the inscription "Proclaim Liberty throughout all the land." It was housed in Independence Hall. It became a symbol of American independence and abolition. For 10 points, name this bell.

Riders on this mail service, started in 1860, carried letters between Missouri and California on horseback. Riders changed horses at relay stations. It ended after the telegraph connected the coasts. For 10 points, name this short-lived western mail service.

This white marble mausoleum in Agra was built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. It has a large dome and four minarets. It sits beside the Yamuna River. For 10 points, name this Indian landmark.

This large ancient arena in Rome hosted gladiator fights. Construction was finished under the emperor Titus in 80 CE. Its official name was the Flavian Amphitheater. For 10 points, name this oval stadium in Rome.

This Incan citadel sits high in the Andes above the Urubamba River in Peru. Hiram Bingham brought it to world attention in 1911. Its terraced stone buildings were built in the fifteenth century. For 10 points, name this ruin near Cusco.

This prehistoric ring of standing stones stands on Salisbury Plain in England. Its largest stones are arranged in a circle with horizontal lintels. Some blue stones were moved from Wales. For 10 points, name this monument.

This magnetic instrument has a needle that always points north. Sailors used it for navigation beginning in medieval times. It was invented in China. For 10 points, name this tool that helps travelers find direction.

This Polish-born scientist was the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. She discovered polonium and radium with her husband Pierre. For 10 points, name this woman who won in both physics and chemistry.

This German-born physicist developed the theory of relativity and the equation E equals m c squared. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921 for the photoelectric effect. He moved to Princeton in 1933. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This woman lost her sight and hearing as an infant but graduated from Radcliffe College. Her teacher Anne Sullivan spelled words into her hand. She wrote The Story of My Life. For 10 points, name this American author and activist.

This painter, sculptor, and inventor drew the Vitruvian Man and sketched flying machines. He painted The Last Supper and was born in the town of Vinci. His notebooks are written in mirror writing. For 10 points, name this Italian Renaissance polymath.

This American astronaut was the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969, as commander of Apollo 11. His words included "one small step for man." He was joined by Buzz Aldrin. For 10 points, name this astronaut.

This woman was the first female pilot to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean, in 1932. She disappeared over the Pacific in 1937 during an attempt to fly around the world. Her navigator was Fred Noonan. For 10 points, name this aviator.

This American statesman is pictured on the hundred-dollar bill. He flew a kite in a thunderstorm, invented bifocals and the lightning rod, and published Poor Richard's Almanack. For 10 points, name this founding father.

q: This is the base unit of length in the metric system. It is slightly longer than a yard, and one hundred centimeters make one of these. Track events like the one hundred dash are measured in it. For 10 points, name this unit of length.
This is the base unit of mass in the metric system. It is divided into one thousand grams. It was once defined by a platinum-iridium cylinder kept near Paris. For 10 points, name this unit of mass.

On this temperature scale, water freezes at zero degrees and boils at one hundred degrees at sea level. It is named for a Swedish astronomer. Most of the world uses it for weather reports. For 10 points, name this scale.
This word describes a group of twelve items. Eggs are often sold in this quantity in a carton. Half of it is six, and a baker's one is sometimes thirteen. For 10 points, name this unit.
This word describes a period of ten years. The 1990s and the 1920s are examples. It comes from the Greek word for ten, and it is shorter than a generation. For 10 points, name this unit of time.

This word describes a period of one hundred years. The twentieth one began in 1901 by strict counting. It comes from a Latin word for one hundred, and its adjective is also the name of a plant. For 10 points, name this unit of time.

This system of numerals uses letters such as I, V, X, L, C, D, and M. The letter L stands for fifty in it. It was used in ancient Rome. For 10 points, name this numbering system still seen on clock faces and movie credits.

Melvil Dewey developed this library classification system in 1876. It assigns numbers from 000 to 999 to broad subject areas. Books are shelved by these numbers. For 10 points, name this system used in many school libraries.

Noah Webster published a famous American example of this type of book in 1828. It lists words alphabetically with their meanings, spellings, and pronunciations. The Oxford English one is another well-known example. For 10 points, name this reference work.

L. L. Zamenhof created this constructed language in 1887 as a neutral means of communication between nations. Its name means "one who hopes." It has regular grammar with no irregular verbs. For 10 points, name this artificial language.
This ancient language of Rome gave English many roots, such as aqua and terra. It is the source of the Romance languages. Julius Caesar wrote in it. For 10 points, name this language.

The first letter of this alphabet is alpha and the last is omega. Its letters are used in math and science and fraternity names. It was adapted from the Phoenician script. For 10 points, name this alphabet used in ancient Athens.

This alphabet is used in Russian and Bulgarian and was named for a missionary saint. It includes letters like Ж and Я. It was developed from Greek in the ninth century. For 10 points, name this writing system.

This word names a word with the same meaning as another, such as "big" and "large." The word is formed from Greek parts meaning "together" and "name." A thesaurus lists many of them. For 10 points, name this type of word.

This word names a word that means the opposite of another, such as "hot" and "cold." Its prefix comes from a Greek word meaning "against." A thesaurus often lists these along with synonyms. For 10 points, name this type of word.

This word names a word that reads the same forward and backward. Examples include "level," "radar," and "kayak." Some sentences, such as "Madam, I'm Adam," also have this property. For 10 points, name this kind of word.

This literary term describes a word that imitates a sound, such as "buzz," "splash," or "meow." Its name comes from Greek roots meaning "name making." Comic books use them in bold letters. For 10 points, name this figure of speech.

This is the study of the sounds, lengths, and stresses of speech. Linguists use a special alphabet to write them. Teachers of reading use it to explain how letters map to sounds. For 10 points, name the study of speech sounds.

This document of 1776, written chiefly by Thomas Jefferson, announced the thirteen colonies' separation from Britain. It begins "When in the Course of human events." For 10 points, name this document adopted on July 4.

King John of England was forced to seal this charter in 1215 at Runnymede. It limited royal power and promised the right to a lawful trial. Its name is Latin for "great charter." For 10 points, name this document.
